summary: The note explains fracture zones, linear features on the ocean floor formed by offset mid-ocean ridge segments and plate tectonics, often hundreds to thousands of kilometers long. It distinguishes fracture zones from the transform faults that form them, describes how their age offsets and magnetic striping reveal past plate motion, and gives examples including the Blanco, Charlie-Gibbs, Heirtzler, Mendocino, Romanche and Sovanco fracture zones.
one_line: Overview of fracture zones, linear ocean-floor features from offset mid-ocean ridges, their relation to transform faults, and examples like the Romanche and Mendocino zones.
key_facts: A fracture zone is a linear feature on the ocean floor, often hundreds or even thousands of kilometers long, resulting from offset mid-ocean ridge axis segments.
Fracture zones are usually seismically inactive because both plate segments move in the same direction.
Transform faults are plate boundaries, whereas fracture zones are the junction between oceanic crustal regions of different ages.
Younger crust is generally higher due to increased thermal buoyancy, so a fracture zone is characterized by an offset in elevation.
Past plate motion direction and rate can be determined from offsets in the magnetic striping on the ocean floor, which result from reversals of Earth's magnetic field.
The Blanco Fracture Zone runs between the Juan de Fuca Ridge and the Gorda Ridge and its dominating feature is the 150 km long Blanco Ridge.
The Charlie-Gibbs Fracture Zone consists of two fracture zones in the North Atlantic that extend for over 2000 km and displace the Mid-Atlantic Ridge a total of 350 km to the west.
The Mendocino Fracture Zone extends for over 4,000 km off the coast of California and separates the Pacific Plate and Gorda Plate.
Rocks north of the Mendocino Fracture Zone ridge were found to be 23 to 27 million years younger than those to the south.
The Romanche Fracture Zone, also known as the Romanche Trench, reaches 7,758 m deep, is 300 km long, and is 19 km wide.
The Romanche Fracture Zone offsets the Mid-Atlantic Ridge by more than 640 km.
The Sovanco Fracture Zone is a dextral-slip transform fault between the Juan de Fuca and Explorer Ridge in the North Pacific Ocean, 125 km long and 15 km wide.
The Heirtzler Fracture Zone was approved by the Advisory Committee on Undersea Features in 1993.
Fracture zones are usually defined with bathymetric, gravity and magnetic studies.
